SCENE CARD (updated 06:00:00)
Location: High Street, Camden, London
Incident type: Stop and search — suspected possession of controlled drugs
Subjects: 1 male, ~20s, agitated, raised voice once
Officer: PC Aservda, 2 years experience
Duration: 1m 05s
Key facts: Officer reports a strong smell of cannabis from the subject's clothing. Subject has hands in pockets, asks why he has been stopped.
Weather: Night, clear, 9°C
Escalation index: 0.35 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: Do I have grounds to search this person, and what must I tell them first?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 2
Certs: Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: 1 (verbal warning, 6 months prior)

<think>
The officer reports a strong smell of cannabis emanating from the subject's clothing. Under s.23(2) Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, a constable who has reasonable grounds to suspect a person is in possession of a controlled drug may search that person and detain them for the purpose of the search. Cannabis is a controlled drug, and possession is restricted under s.5 MDA 1971. The smell of cannabis can contribute to reasonable grounds, but current guidance (Code A) requires the suspicion to be objective and not based on a single factor alone where avoidable; here the strong smell from the clothing is a specific, articulable factor that can found reasonable suspicion. The grounds must be genuine and objective — not based on the subject's demeanour, agitation, or ethnicity.

Before searching, the officer must comply with PACE Code A para 3.8 — the GOWISELY requirements: Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a copy of the record, Legal power, and that You are detained for the search. The officer must take reasonable steps to give this information before the search begins.

The subject is agitated and has hands in pockets. There's a personal safety dimension, but the proportionate posture is to explain clearly and calmly, ask the subject to take hands out of pockets for safety, and reduce tension. The subject asking "why have I been stopped" is an opportunity to deliver the grounds clearly, which itself de-escalates.

This is a street search, not an arrest, so Code C custody rights (s.56/s.58 PACE) don't yet apply unless the person is arrested and taken to a station. The relevant immediate right is entitlement to a copy of the search record.

I must not opine on guilt. Escalation risk is medium given agitation, hands in pockets, night-time, but contained.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, s.23(2)(a) gives a constable power to search a person, and to detain them for that purpose, where the constable has reasonable grounds to suspect possession of a controlled drug in contravention of the Act (possession being restricted by s.5). A strong smell of cannabis from the subject's clothing is a specific, articulable factor capable of contributing to reasonable grounds, provided the suspicion is genuine and objective and not founded on demeanour, agitation, or appearance alone. Before searching, PACE Code A para 3.8 requires you to take reasonable steps to convey the GOWISELY elements (Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a copy of the record, Legal power, and that the person is detained for a search). Anything found that appears to be evidence may be seized under s.23(2)(c).", "suggested_action": "You may form reasonable grounds to search under s.23(2) MDA 1971 if you can articulate the specific smell of cannabis from the subject's clothing as your objective ground, separate from his demeanour. Before any search, consider clearly delivering all GOWISELY elements required by Code A para 3.8 — particularly stating the grounds (the smell) and the legal power. Consider asking the subject to take his hands out of his pockets for everyone's safety, explaining why, before commencing. You may seize and detain under s.23(2)(c) anything found that appears to be evidence of an offence.", "tone_guidance": "Speak slowly and calmly at a steady volume; the subject's question 'why have I been stopped' is an opening, not a challenge — answer it directly with the grounds, which often lowers tension. Acknowledge that being stopped is frustrating, explain that this is a brief procedure, and tell him what will happen next. Avoid mirroring his raised voice. Keep your request to remove hands from pockets framed as a mutual safety step rather than an accusation.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "This is a street search under s.23 MDA 1971, not an arrest, so PACE Code C custody rights are not yet engaged; however the subject is entitled to a copy of the search record (Code A para 3.8). The search must be limited to what is reasonably required to find the suspected drugs, conducted with proper regard to the subject's rights, and you may only detain him for as long as is reasonably necessary to carry it out. Your power depends on genuine reasonable suspicion; without it the detention is unlawful. If, following the search, you arrest and take him to a station, the custody officer must then inform him of his rights to have someone told of his arrest (s.56 PACE) and to free independent legal advice (s.58 PACE) under Code C para 3.1.", "next_steps": ["Articulate and, where practicable, note the specific objective grounds (strong smell of cannabis from clothing) before commencing the search", "Deliver all GOWISELY elements under Code A para 3.8 and confirm the subject understands, then ask him to remove his hands from his pockets for safety", "Conduct the search proportionately and limited to its object; if items are found, consider seizure under s.23(2)(c) MDA 1971", "Complete and offer a copy of the search record to the subject", "If the search results in arrest, ensure on arrival at custody the subject is informed of his s.56 and s.58 PACE rights per Code C para 3.1"]}

SCENE CARD (updated 22:10:50)
Location: High Street, Camden, London
Incident type: Member of public filming officers
Subjects: 1 male, ~teens, nervous, glancing around
Officer: PC Doyle, 3 years experience
Duration: 5m 50s
Key facts: A bystander is filming the incident on a phone and standing a few metres back. The bystander is not obstructing officers.
Weather: Night, drizzle, 7°C
Escalation index: 0.25 (LOW)

QUERY: Can I require the bystander to stop filming or hand over the phone?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 3
Certs: Mental Health First Aid, Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: None

<think>
The officer is asking whether a bystander filming police in a public street can be required to stop filming or hand over their phone. This is England & Wales law.

Key principle: There is no general power to require a member of the public to stop filming officers in a public place, nor to seize their phone simply because it contains footage of police. The bystander is standing a few metres back and is not obstructing officers — so there is no obstruction offence (no basis under, e.g., obstructing an officer).

The Wood v Commissioner of Police case discusses Article 8 and overt photography in public — it recognises that in a public street people may take photographs at any time, and that there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in such a setting. The same logic supports that members of the public may film in public. Wood notes that police themselves film overtly and openly; the converse — the public filming police — is lawful activity in a public place. The film of officers performing public duties does not engage any seizure power.

There is no power here to seize the phone. Seizure would require a lawful basis (e.g. the device being evidence of an offence, or a relevant statutory seizure power following a lawful search). The bystander is not suspected of an offence on these facts. There is no search power engaged (no section 60 authorisation mentioned, no reasonable suspicion under PACE Code A). If the officer were to conduct any search, GOWISELY under PACE Code A para 3.8 would apply, but there's no lawful ground to search here.

So the guidance: the officer may not lawfully require the bystander to stop filming, and may not seize the phone absent a lawful basis. Filming officers in public is lawful. The officer should not interfere unless the bystander begins to obstruct, harass, or commit an offence. De-escalation: acknowledge the filming is permitted, maintain professional conduct, do not be drawn into confrontation. The subject is teenage and nervous — sensitive approach needed.

Escalation risk is low (index 0.25, bystander not obstructing).

Rights reminder: freedom to record in public, no requirement to stop or surrender device, Article 8/expression considerations.

Cite: Wood v Commissioner of Police [2009] EWCA Civ 414 (public-place photography, no reasonable expectation of privacy, overt filming). PACE Code A para 3.8 (GOWISELY) only relevant if any search were contemplated. PACE Code A 2.14A-2.14B re section 60 — only if such authorisation existed. I should make clear no such basis exists here.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "There is no general police power to require a member of the public to stop filming, or to seize their phone, simply because they are recording officers carrying out duties in a public place. Wood v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis [2009] EWCA Civ 414 confirms that in a public street people may take photographs at any time and there is generally no reasonable expectation of privacy in that setting; the court also notes that police filming in public is conducted overtly and openly. The reciprocal filming of officers in public is lawful activity. Seizure of a device or any search of the person would require a specific lawful basis: a search power under PACE Code A would require the GOWISELY safeguards in para 3.8 (Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a record, Legal power, You are detained), and a suspicion-less search such as section 60 of the CJPOA 1994 would require a prior inspector-rank authorisation under PACE Code A paras 2.14A-2.14B. On the facts presented, none of those bases appears to be engaged.", "suggested_action": "You may continue with the incident without interfering with the bystander, who is several metres back and not obstructing you. Consider treating the filming as lawful and unremarkable. You may not lawfully require them to stop filming, delete footage, or hand over the phone in these circumstances, as no search power, seizure power, or offence appears to be in play. If at any point the person physically obstructs you or the conduct moves beyond filming, consider reassessing against the specific power that would then apply.", "tone_guidance": "Stay calm, professional and unprovoked by the camera. Consider acknowledging that filming in public is permitted and that you have no issue with it. Given the subject appears young and nervous, a measured, non-confrontational manner will reduce tension. Avoid moving towards the phone, demanding identification, or issuing instructions that have no legal basis, as that risks escalating a presently low-risk situation.", "escalation_risk": "low", "rights_reminder": "The bystander is entitled to film officers in a public place and is under no obligation to stop, explain themselves, identify themselves, or surrender their device absent a lawful power. Any interference with their phone would engage their rights and require a specific legal basis. The officer's powers do not extend to compelling deletion of footage or seizing the device on these facts.", "next_steps": ["Continue managing the primary incident and maintain professional conduct on the assumption you may be recorded.", "Do not instruct the bystander to stop filming or hand over the phone, as no lawful basis is identified.", "Monitor whether the bystander moves from observing to obstructing, harassing, or committing an offence, and reassess the applicable power only if that occurs.", "If any search or seizure later becomes lawful, deliver the GOWISELY information under PACE Code A para 3.8 before acting and record the grounds.", "Note the encounter and the bystander's conduct in your pocket notebook for accurate later reference."]}

SCENE CARD (updated 23:59:07)
Location: Briggate, Leeds city centre
Incident type: Use of force — proportionality assessment
Subjects: 2 subjects, both male ~20s; one agitated, one passive
Officer: PS Whitfield, 11 years experience
Duration: 0m 45s
Key facts: A subject is resisting being handcuffed after a lawful detention. He appears distressed and may have a vulnerability. He is not striking out.
Weather: Morning, foggy, 5°C
Escalation index: 0.67 (HIGH)

QUERY: The subject appears vulnerable. How does that affect my use of force?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 11
Certs: Public Order Level 2, Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: None

<think>
The officer is dealing with a subject who is resisting handcuffing after a lawful detention. The subject appears distressed and possibly vulnerable, but is NOT striking out — i.e., passive resistance rather than active aggression.

Step 1 — Power to use force. Section 117 PACE permits a constable to use "reasonable force, if necessary" in exercising PACE powers. The Criminal Law Act 1967 principle (reasonable force to effect arrest) also applies. But the key word is "reasonable" and "necessary."

Step 2 — Handcuffing is not automatic. AB v Chief Constable of North Wales [2026] EWCC 11 makes clear that handcuffing on arrest is not an automatic right. The College of Policing Guidance (cited in that case) requires restraint be a last resort, the minimum necessary, applied for the shortest time necessary. Okoro shows that handcuffing based on build/"unknown risk" alone, where the person has not been violent, was held insufficient. Gilchrist: where there are sufficient officers, less need for force. The subject here is not striking out — so the threshold for restraint and degree of force must be carefully justified.

Step 3 — Vulnerability. This is the crux. Commissioner of Police v ZH [2013] EWCA Civ 69 is directly on point. Where a subject is or may be vulnerable (e.g. autistic, epileptic, mentally impaired), officers have a continuing duty to make reasonable adjustments and must take into account vulnerability. Restraint of a vulnerable person, if prolonged or disproportionate, can amount to inhuman/degrading treatment under Article 3 HRA 1998. The MCA section 5/6 framework: acts done for a person lacking capacity in their best interests, and restraint only if reasonably believed necessary to prevent harm AND proportionate. The whole duration of restraint matters, not just the application.

Step 4 — Distress / possible vulnerability means the resistance may stem from fear or sensory overload, not defiance. De-escalation is the proportionate first response. Slowing down, communicating clearly, giving the subject time, reducing the number of officers crowding may achieve compliance without further force.

Step 5 — Safeguards: continuing duty to reassess necessity moment-by-moment; reasonable adjustments; minimum force for shortest time; Article 3 threshold; if no continuing risk, the justification for restraint falls away.

Escalation risk: medium — subject is distressed and resisting but not striking out; risk of the situation escalating if force is applied without adjustment, and risk of Article 3 breach.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "Force in exercise of PACE powers must be 'reasonable, if necessary': s.117 PACE 1984 (AB v Chief Constable of North Wales Police [2026] EWCC 11). Handcuffing/restraint is not an automatic right on arrest or detention and must be a last resort, the minimum necessary and applied for the shortest time necessary (College of Policing guidance cited in AB v Chief Constable of North Wales Police [2026] EWCC 11; Okoro v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2011] EWHC 0003 (QB); Gilchrist v Chief Constable of Greater Manchester Police [2019] EWHC 1233 (QB)). Where a subject is or may be vulnerable there is a continuing duty to make reasonable adjustments, and disproportionate or prolonged restraint of a vulnerable person can breach Article 3 ECHR / Human Rights Act 1998, assessed over the whole period of restraint, not just at the point handcuffs are applied (Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis v ZH [2013] EWCA Civ 69).", "suggested_action": "Given the subject is distressed, possibly vulnerable and is not striking out, you may wish to pause the handcuffing and treat his apparent vulnerability as a factor that raises the threshold for, and reduces the proportionality of, any further force. Consider whether continued restraint is genuinely necessary at this moment to prevent harm; if it is, consider applying only the minimum force for the shortest time. Consider using available officers to provide reassurance and space rather than to overpower, and consider making reasonable adjustments to your communication and approach to account for the possible vulnerability.", "tone_guidance": "Slow the pace and lower your voice. Distress-driven resistance is often fear or sensory overload rather than defiance, so consider giving short, simple explanations of what you are doing and why, allow processing time, avoid crowding, and explain that you are trying to keep him safe. Calm, low-stimulus communication is itself a de-escalation and proportionality measure and may achieve compliance without further force.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "The subject retains the protection of Article 3 against inhuman or degrading treatment; force and restraint must be proportionate across the whole period it is used, not just at the outset. He is entitled to be told the fact and grounds of his detention/arrest as soon as it is practicable to do so (s.28(3) PACE; Christie v Leachinsky [1947] AC 573, as applied in Dilon Curwen v Chief Constable of Cumbria [2026] EWHC 115 (KB)). Your power to use force is limited to what is reasonable and necessary (s.117 PACE); the necessity for restraint must be kept under continuous review and any reasonable belief about his best interests or the need to restrain must take account of his vulnerability (Commissioner of Police v ZH [2013] EWCA Civ 69).", "next_steps": ["Reassess in real time whether restraint remains necessary to prevent harm to the subject or others, and document your reasoning.", "Make reasonable adjustments for the possible vulnerability — simplify communication, allow time, and consider summoning medical or mental health support.", "Ensure the fact and grounds of detention have been communicated clearly as soon as it is practicable for him to understand them.", "If restraint is applied, keep it to the minimum and shortest duration, monitor the subject's welfare continuously, and record the duration and justification.", "Note the distress and suspected vulnerability in your account and consider an early welfare/medical assessment if he is taken into custody."]}

SCENE CARD (updated 17:35:55)
Location: Lord Street, Liverpool
Incident type: Public disturbance — possible breach of the peace
Subjects: 2 subjects, both male ~20s; one agitated, one passive
Officer: PC Aservda, 2 years experience
Duration: 0m 45s
Key facts: Two neighbours are in a heated argument in the street; one has squared up to the other. No blows have been struck. A small crowd is gathering.
Weather: Morning, foggy, 5°C
Escalation index: 0.5 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: How long can I hold someone to prevent further disorder?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 2
Certs: Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: None

<think>
The officer is dealing with a possible breach of the peace: two men arguing, one squaring up, no blows yet, crowd gathering. The question is about how long someone can be held to prevent further disorder.

Relevant power: common law power to take action to prevent an imminent or ongoing breach of the peace. The key principle from R (Hicks) v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis [2017] UKSC 9 is that preventive detention is lawful where reasonably considered necessary to prevent the person committing an offence/breach of the peace, and crucially that detention must last only as long as the risk persists — early release once the risk has passed is lawful and indeed preferable. There is no fixed clock; the detention is justified only for the duration of the imminent risk. The officer can detain to prevent an imminent breach where there isn't time to give a warning, but the threshold is imminence and the response must be proportionate.

So the answer to "how long" is: only for as long as the imminent risk of a breach of the peace persists, and the person should be released as soon as the risk has passed. If the situation can't resolve quickly and continued detention is needed, then they would need to be brought before magistrates to be bound over — but the Hicks principle makes clear that early release once danger passes is lawful and the preferred route. This is a short, dynamic situation (45 seconds, no blows). De-escalation and separation are the proportionate first step.

Necessity test under PACE Code G applies if moving to a section 24 arrest for a substantive offence (e.g. preventing physical harm/damage). But breach of the peace is a common law preventive power, not section 24. I should not overstate — describe necessity principles for arrest.

Proportionality of any force: Curwen [2026] EWHC 115 (KB) — force must be objectively reasonable and proportionate to the threat. No force needed yet here; verbal de-escalation and separation first.

Rights: if a person is taken into custody at a station, PACE Code C para 3.1 rights apply (s.56, s.58). But for a brief preventive hold on the street, the limit is that detention only lasts as long as the imminent risk.

Escalation risk: medium — squaring up, crowd gathering, but no blows, short duration.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "At common law you have a power to take reasonable steps, including detention, to prevent a breach of the peace that is occurring or reasonably and imminently apprehended. The duration of any such preventive detention is governed by the principle in R (Hicks) v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis [2017] UKSC 9: detention to prevent a person committing an offence/breach of the peace is lawful only for as long as the imminent risk persists, and releasing the person as soon as the risk has passed (rather than holding them to take them before a court) is lawful and indeed the preferred course. There is no fixed period — the lawful duration is dictated by the continuing necessity, not a clock. The Court recognised that police may act where there is not sufficient time to give a warning. If you instead move to arrest for a substantive offence, the two-part test in PACE Code G paras 2.4-2.9 applies (reasonable grounds to suspect involvement in an offence AND reasonable grounds to believe arrest is necessary, e.g. to prevent physical harm or to ascertain a name/address). Any use of force must be objectively reasonable and proportionate to the threat as it presents: Dilon Curwen v Chief Constable of Cumbria [2026] EWHC 115 (KB).", "suggested_action": "You may treat any hold purely as preventive: detain only for as long as the imminent risk of a breach of the peace genuinely persists, and consider releasing the moment tempers have cooled and the risk has passed — you are not obliged to hold someone for any minimum period. Consider separating the two men so they are out of each other's sight and line, dispersing or moving back the gathering crowd, and giving the agitated subject a clear chance to calm before contemplating any physical intervention. If, after de-escalation, the risk remains and you judge a substantive arrest necessary, you may then work through the Code G necessity criteria before acting.", "tone_guidance": "Use a calm, low and steady voice; address the agitated subject by name if known and keep your stance open and non-confrontational. Acknowledge the dispute without taking sides, set out simple choices ('let's step back over here so we can sort this out'), and create physical and visual separation between the parties. Avoid commands that escalate; explain what you are doing and why. Keep the passive subject reassured so the situation does not flip.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "Any preventive hold must be the minimum necessary and must end as soon as the imminent risk dissipates — you cannot detain to punish or simply because an argument occurred. The subjects retain their liberty under Article 5 and may only be deprived of it on the recognised grounds and for no longer than necessary. If anyone is taken into custody at a station, PACE Code C para 3.1 rights are engaged: the right to have someone informed (s.56 PACE), the right to free independent legal advice (s.58 PACE), and access to the Codes. Do not express any view on who is at fault in the dispute.", "next_steps": ["Separate the two subjects and create distance between them and the gathering crowd to remove the trigger for further disorder", "Continuously reassess whether the imminent risk still exists and be prepared to release immediately once it has passed, recording your rationale and timings on BWV", "If de-escalation fails and you judge detention or arrest necessary, work through the Code G necessity criteria and articulate which ground applies before acting", "Document the grounds for any preventive hold, the duration, and the point at which the risk subsided, noting any decision to release early", "Call for support if the crowd grows or the agitated subject's behaviour escalates, and only use force that is reasonable and proportionate to the threat then presented"]}

SCENE CARD (updated 18:24:12)
Location: St Peter's Street, Manchester
Incident type: Custody — detainee rights and caution
Subjects: 1 male, ~20s, agitated, raised voice once
Officer: PS Calloway, 14 years experience
Duration: 1m 05s
Key facts: Subject has just been brought into custody. He is asking whether he has to answer questions and whether he can get a solicitor.
Weather: Night, clear, 9°C
Escalation index: 0.35 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: What rights must I make sure this detainee is told about?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 14
Certs: Custody-trained, PACE-trained
Prior incidents at location: 1 (verbal warning, 6 months prior)

<think>
The officer's query is about a detainee newly brought into custody who is asking two specific things: (1) whether he has to answer questions, and (2) whether he can get a solicitor. This is a Code C detainee-rights situation.

Relevant law: PACE Code C para 3.1 sets out what the custody officer must tell the detainee on arrival — the right to have someone informed (s.56 PACE), the right to consult privately with a solicitor and that free independent legal advice is available (s.58 PACE), and the right to consult the Codes of Practice. Code C para 6.1 reinforces the right to consult and communicate privately with a solicitor at any time, in person, in writing, or by telephone, free of charge.

On "does he have to answer questions" — the caution and the right to silence. CJPOA 1994 s.34 governs adverse inferences from failure to mention facts later relied on. Crucially s.34(2A) provides that where the accused was at an authorised place of detention, inferences cannot be drawn if he had not been allowed an opportunity to consult a solicitor before questioning. So the right to silence exists, but adverse inferences may follow in certain circumstances — and access to legal advice protects against inferences. I should not advise on guilt; I just lay out the rights neutrally.

s.58 detail: request to consult a solicitor must be recorded in custody record, must be permitted as soon as practicable, and within 36 hours. Delay only for indictable offence, authorised by superintendent, on the specified grounds. s.56 delay authorised by inspector.

The detainee is agitated, raised voice once, escalation index 0.35 ELEVATED. My own assessment: medium — he's agitated but cooperative-ish, asking questions, no violence indicated.

Posture: explain calmly, ensure custody officer (this is a custody context — PS Calloway) communicates the rights clearly, document the request.

I must phrase as guidance, cite only from snippets. The right to silence/caution I can describe in principle; s.34 is in the snippets for the inference point and the s.34(2A) solicitor protection.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "PACE Code C, para 3.1 requires that on arrival in custody the detainee be told clearly of the right to have someone informed of his arrest (s.56 PACE 1984), the right to consult privately with a solicitor and that free independent legal advice is available (s.58 PACE 1984), and the right to consult the Codes of Practice. PACE Code C, para 6.1 confirms the detainee may at any time consult and communicate privately with a solicitor in person, in writing or by telephone, free of charge. Under s.58 PACE 1984 a request for a solicitor and its time must be recorded in the custody record (s.58(2)) and the detainee must be permitted to consult as soon as practicable (s.58(4)) and in any event within 36 hours (s.58(5)); delay is permitted only for an indictable offence and only if authorised by a superintendent on the limited grounds in s.58(8). Under s.56 any delay to having someone informed requires inspector authorisation on the equivalent grounds. On whether he must answer questions: he has the right to silence, but under CJPOA 1994 s.34 a court may in certain circumstances draw inferences from a failure to mention a fact later relied on in his defence; importantly s.34(2A) provides that no such inference may be drawn if he had not been allowed an opportunity to consult a solicitor before questioning.", "suggested_action": "You may ensure the custody officer delivers the full rights notification under Code C para 3.1 in clear terms the detainee understands, covering the s.56 right to have someone informed, the s.58 right to free private legal advice, and access to the Codes. In answer to his questions, you may explain that he is entitled to free independent legal advice at any time (Code C para 6.1) and that, while he is not obliged to answer questions, the caution explains the position; consider not commencing any questioning until he has had the opportunity to consult a solicitor if he wants one, given the protection in s.34(2A). Consider recording his request for a solicitor and its time in the custody record as required by s.58(2).", "tone_guidance": "Speak slowly and calmly, acknowledging his agitation without matching it. Frame the rights as protections that exist for him, not as procedural formalities. Confirm he has understood by inviting him to ask anything that is unclear, and reassure him that legal advice is free and confidential. A measured, explanatory tone is likely to reduce the tension already noted.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "The detainee has the right to have a friend, relative or other interested person informed of his arrest (s.56), the right to consult a solicitor privately and free of charge at any time (s.58 / Code C para 6.1), the right to consult the Codes of Practice, and the right to silence. These rights may be exercised as soon as practicable; access to a solicitor can only be delayed for an indictable offence on superintendent authorisation under s.58(8), and informing a named person only on inspector authorisation under s.56. He cannot lawfully be compelled to answer questions, and adverse inferences under s.34 are constrained where he has not had the opportunity to consult a solicitor (s.34(2A)).", "next_steps": ["Ensure the custody officer gives, or has given, the full Code C para 3.1 rights notification and confirm comprehension", "Record any request for a solicitor and the time it was made in the custody record per s.58(2), and facilitate that consultation as soon as practicable", "Refrain from questioning until any requested legal advice has been provided, to preserve the s.34(2A) safeguard", "Document the rights given, his responses and his demeanour on the custody record", "Continue to monitor the detainee's welfare and agitation level and reassess if his behaviour changes"]}
